problemText: A weather reporter on the evening news says: 'Right now, the temperature is 12 degrees Celsius and it is raining.' Is this a weather statement or a climate statement, and why?
choices: It is a climate statement because the reporter is giving information about rain and temperature.
It is a weather statement because it describes the atmosphere at a specific moment in time, not an average across many years.
It is a climate statement because rain and temperature collected over time establish what a region's typical conditions are.
It is a weather statement because the words 'right now' indicate a single point in time rather than a long-term pattern.
hints: Ask yourself: does this describe what is happening RIGHT NOW at one moment, or does it describe a pattern built from many years of records?
Look for timescale clues in the sentence — words like 'right now' or 'average' or 'typical' tell you whether you are looking at weather or climate.

problemText: A student writes: 'Yesterday it was 28 degrees Celsius and sunny in my town, so my town's climate must be warm and dry.' Explain what is wrong with this reasoning.
choices: The student is confusing climate with latitude, which determines whether a place is warm or cold.
The student is correct — a warm, sunny day is the best evidence of a warm, dry climate in any region.
The student is confusing one day of weather with a long-term climate pattern; climate requires many years of averaged records, not a single day.
The student should have said 'yesterday's weather' instead of 'my town's climate,' but the conclusion about the climate is still correct.
hints: Climate is defined by averaging records over how many years — one day, one week, or many decades?
Could a region have a cold, wet climate overall but still have one warm, sunny day? Think about whether that one day would prove the climate is warm and dry.

problemText: A town's official climate records, collected over 35 years, show that summer temperatures average 26 degrees Celsius. On one summer day this year, the temperature reaches 38 degrees Celsius. Which description is correct?
choices: The 38-degree day changes the town's climate record because one hot day proves the climate is getting hotter over the full period.
The 38-degree day means the town's climate record will now show an average of 32 degrees Celsius instead of 26 degrees Celsius when recalculated.
The 38-degree day raises the overall average slightly because adding one new temperature reading of 38 degrees will shift the total sum used in calculating the mean.
The 38-degree day is unusual weather for that town, but by itself it does not change the long-term climate average that was built from 35 years of data.
hints: Does one reading on one day change an average that was built from thousands of daily readings across 35 years?
Climate is the average; weather is the actual conditions on any one day. Can an unusual weather event replace a multi-decade average all by itself?

problemText: Three pieces of information are given about Location F: (1) 'Today, the wind is gusting up to 40 kilometers per hour.' (2) 'Over the last 30 years, Location F's average wind speed has been 15 kilometers per hour.' (3) 'Last week, Location F had three days of rain in a row.' Which statement or statements describe Location F's climate, and why do the others not?
choices: Only statement 2 describes climate because it is based on 30 years of averaged records; statements 1 and 3 describe specific short-term conditions, not an average.
Statements 1 and 3 both describe climate because they document actual wind speeds and precipitation events that represent the typical weather patterns at that location.
Only statement 1 describes climate because it measures wind speed in kilometers per hour, which is the standard unit that climate scientists use to quantify atmospheric conditions.
Statements 2 and 3 describe climate together because one provides the long-term average wind speed and one gives a specific rainfall event that illustrates how that average behaves in practice.
hints: Look at the timescale in each statement: which one names a long span with the word 'average,' and which ones name a specific day or short period?
Climate requires averaged records from many years to be properly defined. Does a single day's wind, or three consecutive days of rain, give you enough data to know the long-term average?

problemText: Location G has a climate described as 'dry, with very little rain.' One winter, Location G receives twice as much rain as it normally does in an entire year, spread across the season. A scientist checks Location G's 50-year climate records before and after that winter and finds the climate description remains unchanged at 'dry, with very little rain.' Explain why the unusually rainy winter did not change Location G's official climate description.
choices: The scientist made an error; a winter with twice the normal yearly rain should have changed the climate description because any increase in precipitation alters the official classification.
One season of above-average rain is weather, not climate. Climate is defined by a 50-year average of all years together, and one season cannot overpower 49 other years of records.
The climate description did not change because the extra rain was spread across the whole season rather than concentrated in one month, so it had less impact on the yearly total.
The winter did change the climate temporarily, but the long-term records automatically adjusted back to the original description after that season ended and new years were added to the average.
hints: What timescale defines climate — one season or many years averaged together?
If 49 years of dry data are already averaged into the 50-year record, how much weight does one season of extra rain have in that average?

problemText: A student makes four claims about two locations that both have 'cold, snowy climates' based on 40 years of averaged records: Claim A: 'Both locations will have snow on the ground every single day of winter.' Claim B: 'Both locations must have at least one day next winter when it is not snowing.' Claim C: 'A record-breaking warm day could occur in either location's upcoming winter and would disprove its climate classification.' Claim D: 'Both locations' official climate records would only change if their typical winter conditions shifted across many future years.' Which claim correctly reflects the relationship between weather and climate for these two locations?
choices: Claim A, because a snowy climate means it snows all the time without exception on every day of every winter.
Claim B, because a snowy climate does not guarantee continuous snow, only that snow is typical across many winters overall.
Claim D and also Claim B together, because climates can vary day to day but only change when the long-term average shifts, and a climate does not promise every single day matches the pattern.
Claim C, because a single warm day anywhere in the region's upcoming winter would prove that the snowy climate classification was incorrect from the start.
hints: A climate statement describes the typical pattern across many years; does it predict what must happen on every single day, or what usually happens overall?
If one unusual day of weather could overturn a 40-year climate average, how stable could any climate classification ever be?

problemText: A surface current is defined as a stream of ocean water that flows along a fairly fixed, repeating path. Which statement best describes what this means about a surface current's behavior?
choices: It moves in all directions at once, spreading water evenly across the entire ocean.
It changes direction randomly each season depending on storm activity.
It only flows during warm months and stops during cold months.
It follows the same route year after year, similar to how a river channel stays in one place.
hints: Think about what 'fixed path' and 'repeating' tell you about consistency.
A river is used as a comparison in the definition—what property of a river does a surface current share?

problemText: The Peru Current flows south along the western coast of South America, carrying cold water from the Antarctic region toward the equator. Based on the definition of a cold current, explain why this current would be classified as cold even though it is flowing toward warmer latitudes.
choices: Because it carries water that is colder than the ocean water it is currently flowing through, even though that water is still in the tropics.
Because cold currents only exist at high latitudes and cannot flow toward the equator, so any southward current must be warm regardless of its actual temperature.
Because the water in it starts out at the coldest possible temperature at its source and retains that absolute temperature throughout its entire journey without any warming.
Because it moves more slowly than warm currents do, and slower-moving water loses heat to the surrounding ocean more rapidly, making it colder.
hints: A current's classification depends on a comparison between the current's water and its surroundings—not on latitude or final temperature.
Remember: warm and cold are relative descriptions, not fixed numbers.

problemText: Two coastlines sit at nearly the same latitude. Coastline X has a warm current flowing past it, while Coastline Y has no current running along it. How would you expect their winter climates to compare?
choices: Coastline Y would have milder winters than Coastline X, because moving water cools the surrounding air through evaporation, and currents increase this cooling effect dramatically.
Coastline X would have milder winters than Coastline Y, because the warm offshore water keeps the air warmer than latitude alone would predict.
Both coastlines would have identical winters because they are at the same latitude, and latitude is the only factor that determines whether winters are mild or severe.
Coastline X would be cooler in winter because the water in the current is moving and causes evaporative cooling of the air above it.
hints: A current adds an effect on top of what latitude, elevation, and distance from water already do—it does not replace those factors.
Which coastline receives warmer ocean water nearby, and how does that affect the air above it?

problemText: The North Atlantic Current is the eastward continuation of the Gulf Stream after it bends away from the United States coast. It carries warm water across the Atlantic toward the coast of northwestern Europe. A student observes that Norway's coast, at about 70°N latitude, has much milder winters than most of Canada's coast at the same latitude. Using what you know about how surface currents affect climate, trace the path and effect of the water that creates this difference.
choices: Canada's coast is colder because the cold Labrador Current brings water from the Arctic down along its shoreline, while the North Atlantic Current brings warm tropical water to Norway, and currents override the effect of latitude on coastal climate.

Norway receives warm water because it is positioned on the eastern side of the Atlantic where all European coasts naturally sit in warmer ocean zones, while Canada's western position in North America means it must always have colder coastal conditions regardless of any currents nearby.

The North Atlantic Current carries warm water from the tropical Gulf of Mexico region northeast across the Atlantic, keeping Norwegian coastal air milder than Canada's even though both sit at the same high latitude.

The two coastlines have different climates because the North Atlantic Current carries cold Arctic water to Canada's coast, while a separate warm current from the equator flows directly to Norway, making Norway's climate tropical and Canada's climate polar.
hints: Trace where the warm water in the North Atlantic Current originally came from, and follow it to where it affects Norway's coast.
Remember that a current carries its starting temperature along its entire path—even when far from the tropics, the water is still warmer than its surroundings.

problemText: A cold current and a warm current both flow in opposite directions past the same pair of coastlines. The cold current flows south along Coastline A, carrying Arctic water toward lower latitudes. The warm current flows north along Coastline B, carrying tropical water toward higher latitudes. Both coastlines sit at 45°N latitude. Predict which coastline would have cooler summers and explain your reasoning in terms of the current's origin and the offshore water temperature.
choices: Coastline A would have warmer summers because cold water sinks below the surface and pulls warmer water up from deeper in the ocean to replace it.
Coastline B would have cooler summers because warm currents reflect a large portion of incoming solar radiation back into space, reducing the heat that reaches the coast.
Both coasts would have the same summer temperature because they are at the same latitude, and latitude is the only factor that affects summer warmth.
Coastline A would have cooler summers because the cold current carries water colder than its surroundings, keeping the nearby air cooler than the latitude alone would predict.
hints: Which coastline has colder water sitting next to it, and how does offshore water temperature affect the air above it?
A current's effect depends on whether it is warm (milder than surroundings) or cold (colder than surroundings)—trace this classification from the current's origin.

problemText: Imagine a new warm current suddenly formed and began flowing south along a coastline that had previously received only cold-current water. The coastline's latitude, elevation, and distance from the ocean would stay the same. Using the concept of how currents stack on top of latitude and other geographic factors, explain what would change about the coastline's climate and what would not change.
choices: The coastline's winters and average temperature would become milder than before, because warm offshore water adds a warming effect on top of what latitude and geography already provide. However, the coastline's latitude and general position on Earth would not change.

The coastline would become as warm as tropical regions because warm currents transport equatorial temperatures along with the water, so any place touched by a warm current experiences the same climate as places near the equator.

The coastline's latitude would shift southward over time in response to the warm current, causing the region to eventually match the climate patterns found at lower latitudes where warm currents naturally originate and flow.

Nothing would change about the climate because the current's water would be cooled by the atmosphere before it could affect the coastline, and latitude alone determines whether a region stays cold or becomes warm.
hints: A current does not replace the effects of latitude, elevation, and distance from water—it adds an extra push on top of them. Which of these would actually change, and which would not?
Think about the difference between a place's position on Earth (latitude) and its actual temperature and weather pattern (climate).

problemText: A climatograph shows the typical weather for a location by recording monthly average temperature and monthly average precipitation. These numbers are averaged over many years, not from a single day or single year. Why is it important that the numbers in a climatograph are averages built up from many years rather than from just one year?
choices: Because one year's weather might not show the location's true typical pattern, while many years of data reveal the long-term climate pattern.
Because a single year always has extreme weather in it that would make that year's data unrepresentative of how the location normally behaves overall.
Because scientists need enough data points to measure seasonal patterns accurately, and one year provides insufficient information to identify true climate trends.
Because weather changes constantly within each year, and only by averaging multiple years can scientists smooth out the random variation to find the real average.
hints: Think about the difference between climate (a location's typical pattern) and weather (what happens on a particular day or in a particular year).
If you looked at only one year, could that year have been unusually wet or unusually dry compared to what normally happens?

problemText: A location has these monthly average temperatures in degrees Celsius from January through December: 15, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 25, 25, 23, 20, 17, 16. What is the annual temperature range for this location?
choices: 9 degrees Celsius
10 degrees Celsius
11 degrees Celsius
12 degrees Celsius
hints: The annual temperature range is found by subtracting the coldest month's temperature from the warmest month's temperature.
Scan the twelve numbers to find which month is warmest and which is coldest.

problemText: Location X has the following monthly average precipitation in millimeters from January through December: 120, 110, 95, 60, 40, 25, 20, 22, 35, 55, 85, 105. Does Location X have a strongly marked wet season and dry season, or does it show roughly equal precipitation throughout the year?
choices: It has a dry season from May through September and a wet season from October through April because those months show the clearest difference in precipitation amounts.
It has a wet season only in January and a dry season only in July.
It has a strongly marked dry season from June through August and a strongly marked wet season from November through February.
It has equal precipitation throughout the year because the months with lowest rain still receive at least 20 millimeters, showing that rain falls consistently.
hints: A real wet season is a stretch of several months that is clearly higher than the rest of the year; a real dry season is a stretch clearly lower than the rest.
Look at which groups of months have the highest precipitation numbers and which have the lowest.

problemText: Location M's monthly average temperatures in degrees Celsius from January through December are: 20, 21, 22, 21, 18, 14, 12, 13, 16, 19, 20, 21. Location N's monthly average temperatures in degrees Celsius from January through December are: 12, 11, 8, 4, 0, -4, -6, -5, -1, 4, 9, 12. Both locations show similar patterns of which months are warmer and which are cooler when compared month by month. However, they are in different hemispheres. Why?
choices: Location M is in the Northern Hemisphere because it is warmer than Location N.
Location N is in the Northern Hemisphere because its coldest months occur in June and July.
Location M is in the Southern Hemisphere because its warmest months fall in June, July, and August.
Location N is in the Northern Hemisphere because its coldest months occur in December and January.
hints: The hemisphere is determined by which calendar months are warmest and which are coldest, not by how large the temperature numbers are.
In the Northern Hemisphere, the warmest months are June, July, and August; in the Southern Hemisphere, they are December, January, and February. Which hemisphere's pattern does each location follow?

problemText: A student examines Location P's climatograph and says, 'Location P is very wet because July's precipitation is 180 millimeters.' However, this conclusion is incomplete. Location P's monthly precipitation in millimeters from January through December is: 130, 120, 140, 150, 160, 170, 180, 175, 165, 145, 130, 125. What is wrong with the student's reasoning, and what is a better way to describe Location P's overall wetness?
choices: The student picked out a single month without comparing it to the other eleven months; in fact, Location P receives similar amounts of precipitation every month, so it is wet all year rather than having a special wet season.

The student should have looked at all twelve monthly values to see whether July's 180 millimeters stands out as unusually high or is typical; since most months fall between 120 and 180 millimeters, July is not exceptional.

The student should have checked whether Location P's total annual precipitation is sufficient to classify it as wet, rather than assuming that one high monthly value means the location is very wet year-round.

The student is wrong because he compared only one month to the definition of wetness instead of comparing July's rainfall to the rainfall in the other eleven months to see if July stands out as unusually wet.
hints: Look at all twelve numbers and compare them against each other. Is July's 180 much higher than the other months, or are all the months fairly close together?
A location is not wet because one month is high; it is wet all year if every month stays high, and it has a wet season only if some months are clearly higher than others.

problemText: Location Q and Location R are both in the Northern Hemisphere with the same annual temperature range of 20 degrees Celsius, and both have coldest months in January and warmest months in July. Location Q's monthly precipitation from January through December is: 45, 40, 35, 30, 25, 20, 15, 18, 22, 32, 40, 48. Location R's monthly precipitation from January through December is: 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 90, 95, 90, 20, 5, 5, 5. Both locations receive the same annual precipitation total, but their climate patterns are very different. Calculate the annual precipitation total for each location, then explain why two locations with the same hemisphere, same temperature range, and same total precipitation can still have different climate classifications.
choices: Location Q receives 390 millimeters annually while Location R receives only 310 millimeters annually, so they differ in total wetness and cannot share the same climate classification despite matching temperature ranges.

Both receive 390 millimeters per year; Location Q has no real wet or dry season and stays consistently moist, while Location R has a sharp, concentrated wet season in summer and is dry the rest of the year.
Both receive 390 millimeters per year, but Location Q has more extreme temperature swings than Location R because precipitation is spread throughout the year rather than concentrated in a few months.

Both receive 390 millimeters per year, but Location Q is classified differently because most of its annual precipitation falls between October and December, whereas Location R receives most precipitation between June and August.
hints: Add all twelve numbers for each location to find the annual total. Check your arithmetic carefully—the two totals should be the same.

Once you know the totals are equal, look at how the precipitation is distributed across the year. In one location, is the rain spread fairly evenly across all twelve months? In the other, does most of the rain fall in just a few consecutive months?

problemText: Climate is a region's typical weather pattern averaged over many years. Which of the following is a description of climate rather than weather?
choices: The temperature dropped 8 degrees overnight, which is a single weather event that occurred on one particular night
It rained heavily this morning in the valley, describing a specific precipitation event that happened during a short time period
This region typically stays warm year-round with only small differences between summer and winter
A storm passed through the area last week, which is a weather event that lasted for a brief period and then moved on
hints: Climate looks at patterns over years, not events that happen in days or weeks
Think about the difference between 'typical' and 'what happened today'

problemText: A location sits at 45 degrees north latitude. Why does this location receive sunlight at a lower, more slanting angle compared to a location at the equator?
choices: The curvature of Earth's surface means that at higher latitudes, the same amount of sunlight is spread over a larger area, so the angle becomes more slanting relative to the ground
Locations at high latitudes are tilted away from the sun's rays throughout the entire year, causing the sunlight to strike at a more direct angle
The sunlight has to pass through more atmosphere to reach locations far from the equator, which reduces the angle at which it arrives at the surface
The angle at which sunlight arrives changes with latitude; closer to the poles, sunlight arrives at a lower, more slanting angle rather than close to straight down
hints: Earth's distance from the sun is enormous compared to Earth's size, so latitude does not meaningfully change distance from the sun
What changes with latitude is the angle at which the sunlight arrives, not how far it travels

problemText: Two towns sit in the same mountain valley at the same latitude, but one sits at an elevation of 500 meters above sea level and the other sits at 2,500 meters above sea level. Both towns receive the same amount of sunlight from their latitude. Which town would typically experience colder temperatures, and why?
choices: The town at 2,500 meters, because higher elevation typically results in cooler typical temperatures
The town at 500 meters, because it is closer to the sea and water absorbs heat
Neither town would differ because they share the same latitude and receive the same sunlight
The town at 500 meters, because lower elevation means the air is denser and traps more heat
hints: Elevation is one of three major factors affecting a location's climate, with a clear rule connecting it to temperature
Compare the elevations: which one is higher up, and how does altitude affect temperature?

problemText: Location X sits at low elevation on the coast of a large ocean at 20 degrees north latitude. Location Y sits at the same 20 degrees north latitude and also at low elevation, but 800 kilometers inland with no large body of water nearby. Based on only latitude and distance from water, which location would typically experience larger swings between its hottest and coldest months, and why?
choices: Location X, because being closer to the equator means more extreme seasonal temperature changes
Location Y, because it lacks a nearby large body of water to moderate its temperature throughout the year
Neither location would differ because they share the same latitude and elevation
Location X, because the ocean creates stronger currents that cause temperature to swing more
hints: The latitude and elevation are the same for both, so what remains as a difference between them?
Large bodies of water moderate temperature swings in nearby locations by absorbing and releasing heat slowly throughout the year

problemText: Region P is located at low elevation close to the equator, far inland from any ocean or large lake. Region Q is located at high elevation also close to the equator, but right on the coast of a large ocean. Both regions receive strong, concentrated sunlight from their latitude. Explain why Region P and Region Q would typically have different precipitation patterns, even though both sit close to the equator.
choices: The two regions would have identical precipitation patterns because they share the same latitude and both receive strong sunlight, so all other factors affecting precipitation become irrelevant
Region P receives more precipitation because high elevation reduces the amount of water that falls, while low elevation in Region Q allows less water to accumulate
Region Q receives more precipitation because its coastal location provides a nearby source of moisture, while Region P, being far inland, has less moisture available nearby
Region Q receives less precipitation because the ocean water is too cold to evaporate and supply moisture to the air, which means coastal areas have drier conditions than inland regions
hints: Both regions have the same latitude and sunlight strength, so what differs between them?
Distance from a large body of water affects both the moderation of temperature swings and the amount of moisture available for precipitation

problemText: A geographer is comparing three locations all at exactly the same latitude. Location 1 sits at low elevation on the coast of a large ocean. Location 2 sits at the same low elevation but 1,200 kilometers inland. Location 3 sits at high elevation inland, far from any large body of water. A student predicts that Location 1 would be warmest and Location 3 would be coldest. Another student predicts that both Location 1 and Location 2 would be much warmer than Location 3, but that Locations 1 and 2 would have very similar typical temperatures. Which prediction better matches what the three climate factors would suggest?
choices: The first student's prediction is correct because elevation has a consistent effect on temperature, and coastal locations always retain more heat than inland areas regardless of their distance from the ocean's influence

The first student's prediction is better because it correctly identifies that all three locations differ in at least one climate factor and therefore must all have distinctly different typical temperatures
Both predictions are equally valid because latitude is the only factor that truly determines typical temperature, making the differences between these three locations largely insignificant

The second student's prediction is better because elevation is the strongest factor and would make Location 3 much colder, while distance from water affects temperature moderation and precipitation more than it affects the typical temperature itself
hints: Three factors affect climate: latitude, elevation, and distance from large bodies of water. Think about which factor has the strongest effect on how warm or cold a place typically is

Elevation changes temperature directly, while distance from water moderates temperature swings and affects precipitation. Would this make the typical temperatures of Locations 1 and 2 more similar or very different?
